spoleto.intro: Spoleto's six registered trees sit in places the town has used for centuries: a villa park once owned by a pope, the public gardens on Viale Matteotti, a palace garden by the Roman amphitheatre, the cemetery gate, and the holm-oak wood of Monteluco, protected by a law carved in the 3rd century BC. The pick is the Cedar of Lebanon at Villa Redenta, five to six metres round depending on whose tape you trust. Five of the six stand within an easy walk of the old town; Monteluco takes half a day.
spoleto.meta_description: Six monumental trees in Spoleto, Umbria: the Villa Redenta cedar, a coast redwood by Sol LeWitt's dance floor, and the holm oak of Monteluco.
spoleto.question_meta: Where are the oldest trees in Spoleto?
spoleto.question_answer: Spoleto's oldest trees by any written account are the Cedar of Lebanon in the park of Villa Redenta, described as over 200 years old, and the holm oak at the Franciscan convent on Monteluco, which Umbria's survey calls at least a century old. The Villa Redenta park is public and free, about 1.5 kilometres north of the old town.
spoleto.question_context: Spoleto's trees are measured more carefully than they are dated. Italy's national register gives girth and height for each, and Umbria's own regional survey measured them again, often with slightly different results. The Villa Redenta cedar comes out at 5.2 metres round in one and 6.3 metres in the other. Neither records an age. The Umbrian survey uses the word secolare, which means at least a century and no more, and the only firmer figure is the park's own description of the cedar as over 200 years old. So this page gives ages only where a source does and leaves the rest open. The setting is older than any of the trees. Villa Redenta belonged to Pope Leo XII from 1824 to 1829. The Lex Spoletina, an inscription from the late 3rd century BC, forbade cutting the sacred holm-oak grove on Monteluco, and the convent oak stands inside that wood today. Most of the trees are a short walk from the old town. The plane at Palazzo Marignoli is seen over a garden wall from the lane outside, the redwood and the two cypresses are on public ground, and Monteluco is about 8 kilometres up the road.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Spoleto?
faq.a: The Cedar of Lebanon at Villa Redenta is described as over 200 years old, a round figure rather than a ring count. No other tree here has a firmer date.

faq.q: Are Spoleto's monumental trees free to see?
faq.a: Yes. Villa Redenta's park, the Viale Matteotti gardens, the cemetery and the Monteluco wood are free, the cypress at the Ristorante dei Pini stands at the street gate, and the Palazzo Marignoli plane is seen from the public lane.

faq.q: Can I walk between them?
faq.a: Five of the six are within about 1.5 kilometres of the old town. The holm oak at Monteluco is about 8 kilometres by road above the town, or roughly 4 kilometres by footpath from the Ponte delle Torri.

faq.q: What is the Lex Spoletina?
faq.a: An inscription from the late 3rd century BC that fixed penalties for cutting or burning the sacred holm-oak grove of Monteluco, counted among the earliest forest protection laws.

vallombrosa.intro: Vallombrosa, in the mountains of Reggello above Florence, keeps its big trees in an arboretum started in 1869 so forestry students could experiment with trees from other parts of the world. Two of them are on Italy's national register: a giant sequoia 6.55 metres round and a Lambert pine the register puts at 51.5 metres tall. A short walk up the road stands the Holy Beech, heir to the tree of a legend from 1036, and deeper in the Sant'Antonio forest a twin-trunked beech has a walking loop named after it.
vallombrosa.meta_description: Four monumental trees at Vallombrosa near Florence: a giant sequoia, a 51.5-metre Lambert pine, the Holy Beech and the Faggione of Sant'Antonio.
vallombrosa.question_meta: What are the monumental trees of Vallombrosa?
vallombrosa.question_answer: Vallombrosa has four trees on Italy's national register: a giant sequoia and a Lambert pine inside the experimental arboretum, the Holy Beech beside its chapel near the abbey, and the Faggione in the Sant'Antonio forest. The two arboretum trees are seen only on free guided visits, daily from June to September; the two beeches are on open forest roads and trails.
vallombrosa.question_context: Vallombrosa is a day trip rather than a walk from Florence, about an hour and a quarter by train to Pontassieve and bus 343 up the mountain. What brings people is the abbey and the forest around it, and the trees are part of both. The arboretum was founded in 1869 for the Royal Forestry Institute and moved to its present ground in 1884, and it now holds around 5,000 specimens of more than 700 species. Only two of its trees are on the national register. The giant sequoia stands at the Belvedere delle sequoie among much younger relatives, and the Lambert pine, nicknamed Nazareno, is the one every source measures differently, between 40 and 54 metres. Neither has a published planting date. The Holy Beech is the only tree here with a sourced age: Reggello's tourism office calls it a shoot of the legendary original, about 150 years old, and a trail listing says 120. The Faggione, about 5 metres round and formed from two shoots grown together, stands about 3 kilometres east on the Anello del Faggione and is realistically reached by car. The arboretum cannot be entered unguided, so check the visit times before you travel.

faq.q: Can I visit the Vallombrosa arboretum on my own?
faq.a: No. The arboretum is seen on free guided visits of about 90 minutes, daily from June to September and on request the rest of the year, from beneath the abbey's Torrione.

faq.q: How do I get to Vallombrosa from Florence?
faq.a: Take the train from Santa Maria Novella to Pontassieve, then Autolinee Toscane bus 343 up to Vallombrosa. Allow about an hour and a quarter and check the timetable.

faq.q: What is the Holy Beech?
faq.a: A beech beside the Cappella del Faggio Santo, said to be a shoot of the tree under which Giovanni Gualberto, founder of Vallombrosa, sheltered in March 1036. The standing tree is about 120 to 150 years old.

faq.q: How tall is the Lambert pine?
faq.a: The national register gives 51.5 metres. A guide on a 2023 visit said 54 and a botanical guide says over 40, so the exact figure is disputed.

perugia.intro: Seven of the sixteen trees on this page sit within a kilometre of Perugia's centre, one of the tighter walks on this site, and an eighth, the holm oak that names the courtyard of Santa Giuliana, stands about a kilometre south. Most of the walk is cedars and their relatives, planted through the nineteenth century as the city laid out its public gardens. The rest stand outside town: two country oaks at Prepo, a downy oak up a hillside road, a cypress in Ponte Felcino, and three conifers in the park of Villa del Colle del Cardinale.
perugia.meta_description: Sixteen monumental trees in Perugia: cedars on the old fortress site, the holm oak of Santa Giuliana, and the conifers of Villa del Colle del Cardinale.
perugia.question_meta: Perugia's oldest documented tree is the Palazzo Murena cedar, planted around 1861 in the university's cloister. Where it stands, plus fifteen more.
perugia.question_answer: The oldest tree in Perugia that carries a date is the Cedar of Lebanon in the cloister of Palazzo Murena, planted around 1861 and so roughly 165 years old. It is free to walk in and see, in the courtyard of the university's rectorate in the historic centre. Two others are probably older but undated: the holm oak in the courtyard of Santa Giuliana, which a 2025 event guide calls over 300 years old, and the holm oaks of the Giardini del Frontone, laid out from 1707 and described by a local history piece as already grown when papal troops sacked the city in 1859.
perugia.question_context: Perugia's trees are unusually well recorded for Italy, because most stand on ground the city, the university or the state has managed for over a century. Italy's national register gives girth, height and position and no age, so every date here comes from university records, the comune's pages, local history or the villas' own histories, and where none answers, the age is left blank. Eight of the sixteen are cedars or close relatives, most planted as Perugia laid out the public gardens that replaced the papal fortress. The Frontone entry covers two registered holm oaks about seventy metres apart, so its pin is marked approximate. Four trees, the two Prepo oaks, the Strada dei Conservoni oak and the Ponte Felcino cypress, are register-only, with no second source and no age. The holm oak of Santa Giuliana stands in the courtyard of a monastery founded in 1253, which opens at set times and by reservation. Villa del Colle del Cardinale, a 1575 villa whose gardens reopened in March 2025, holds a big Cedar of Lebanon, a Himalayan cedar and a Monterey cypress behind a small weekend ticket.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Perugia?
faq.a: By documented date, the Palazzo Murena cedar, planted around 1861. The holm oak of Santa Giuliana is said to be over 300 years old and the Frontone holm oaks are probably older too, but nobody has dated them.

faq.q: Are Perugia's monumental trees free to visit?
faq.a: Thirteen of the sixteen are. Seven stand on public squares, streets and gardens in the centre, the cemetery cedar is free, the Santa Giuliana oak is free at set opening times, and the Prepo oaks, the downy oak and the cypress stand on open roads. The three trees at Villa del Colle del Cardinale are behind a small weekend ticket.

faq.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq.a: Seven of the sixteen sit within about a kilometre in the historic centre, with Santa Giuliana about a kilometre south. The cemetery cedar is a short bus ride out, the two Prepo oaks are three kilometres southwest, the downy oak and the cypress stand alone about four kilometres out in opposite directions, and Villa del Colle del Cardinale is about 8 kilometres north-west by car; treat each as its own short trip.

lucca.intro: Lucca keeps most of its best trees inside a ring eight hundred metres across, one of the shortest walks on this site. Three stand in a botanical garden founded in 1820: a cedar from Lebanon, a Californian redwood, and a ginkgo that lightning knocked down and regrew as three trunks. Inside the ring are also a cypress on a gun platform, a cedar with a name, and seven oaks on a tower roof. Two trees beyond the walls repay a drive: the Witches' Oak of Gragnano and a 30-metre Himalayan cedar at Vinchiana.
lucca.meta_description: Sixteen remarkable trees in and around Lucca: seven oaks on the Guinigi tower, the Witches' Oak of Gragnano, and a cedar planted in 1822.
lucca.question_answer: The oldest tree in Lucca with a documented date is the Cedar of Lebanon in the Orto Botanico, planted in 1822 by Paolo Volpi, the garden's first director, which makes it 204 years old and two years younger than the garden around it. It is also one of the largest, at six and a half metres round the trunk. The Witches' Oak of Gragnano, 10 kilometres east, is usually called about 600 years old, but that figure rests on repetition rather than any measurement. The seven holm oaks on top of the Torre Guinigi are the more famous trees, and the idea of planting them up there is far older, but the living oaks are undated replantings.
lucca.question_context: Italy's national register of monumental trees records girth, height and position but no age, so every firm date on this page comes from the botanical garden's own planting records. Those records are unusually good, because the garden was founded as a teaching collection in 1820 by Maria Luisa di Borbone, Duchess of Lucca, and its directors wrote down what they planted and when. They give 1822 for the Cedar of Lebanon and the Corsican pine, 1830 for the magnolia, around 1850 for the redwoods, 1862 for the ginkgo, 1880 for the Balearic box and 1900 for the silver lime. The Torre Guinigi is the exception. A tower crowned with trees appears in Giovanni Sercambi's fifteenth-century chronicle, but the seven holm oaks living there today have been replanted more than once and no source says when. Outside the walls, the Witches' Oak at Gragnano in Capannori carries a legend and an age usually given as about 600 years, with no measurement behind it. The Himalayan cedar at Vinchiana stands 30 metres tall over a cemetery forecourt, with no date at all.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Lucca?
faq.a: The Cedar of Lebanon in the Orto Botanico, planted in 1822 by the garden's first director and now 204 years old. The Witches' Oak at Gragnano is said to be about 600, but nobody has dated it. The oaks on the Torre Guinigi are older as an idea and younger as trees.

faq.q: Can you walk between them?
faq.a: Most of them, and it is a short walk. Thirteen stand inside the city walls within about 800 metres of each other, from the botanical garden in the southeast corner to the Guinigi tower in the middle of the old town. A plane tree on the ramparts near Porta San Donato is a further fifteen to twenty minute walk west along the wall-top path. The Witches' Oak, about 10 kilometres east, and the Vinchiana cedar, about 8 kilometres north, need a car or a bike.

faq.q: Do they cost anything to see?
faq.a: Eight of the sixteen do. Seven stand inside the botanical garden, which charges standard admission, and the Guinigi tower's rooftop oaks cost 8 euro and 230 steps. The other eight, including the cypress on the San Regolo bastion, the cedar at Villa Bottini, the plane on the western walls, the Witches' Oak and the Vinchiana cedar, are free.

faq.q: Are there really trees on top of the Guinigi tower?
faq.a: Seven of them, holm oaks, growing in a walled box of earth 44 metres above the street. They are the emblem of the city and they are the reason people climb the tower.

rome.intro: Rome's noble families turned trees into status symbols the way they turned villas into galleries. Cardinal Scipione Borghese's gardener planted a grove of oriental planes in the 1600s that foresters call the oldest living trees in the city, and the Pamphilj and Mattei families each planted cedars of Lebanon as a shorthand for permanence. Rome has 65 trees registered as monumental under Italian law, more than any other Italian city. The trees here range from a 425-year-old plane to a Mexican desert palm and a holm oak in the square at Ostia Antica, and all but two are free.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Rome?
faq.a: Adonis, a 425-year-old oriental plane in Villa Borghese, is the oldest tree in Rome with a documented planting date. An older oak on the Gianicolo is popularly said to be a thousand years old, but no scientific dating backs the claim.

faq.q: Why does Rome have so many cedars of Lebanon?
faq.a: Roman noble families used them as garden status symbols from the 1600s onward. Villa Doria Pamphilj and Villa Celimontana each planted their own, prizing the species for its biblical associations with endurance and permanence.

faq.q: Are Rome's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Thirty of the thirty-two on this list stand in free public parks, streets and squares, including the holm oak in Piazza Gregoriopoli at Ostia Antica. The other two stand inside ticketed gardens.

faq.q: How does Italy protect its monumental trees?
faq.a: A 2013 national law lets municipalities register trees of exceptional age, size or historical value as monumental. Rome has 65 of them, more than any other Italian city.

florence.intro: Florence's old trees split between two origins. The Giardino dei Semplici, a botanical garden founded in 1545 to grow medicine for the Medici, holds the city's oldest documented trees: a yew planted in 1720 and a cork oak from 1805. Almost everything else dates from the 1860s and 70s, when Florence briefly served as capital of Italy and Giuseppe Poggi laid out new parks and viewpoints above the Arno. One survivor belongs to neither: a wisteria of about 200 years, the last of a villa pergola, now in a supermarket forecourt on Via Pisana.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Florence?
faq.a: A European yew in the Giardino dei Semplici botanical garden, planted in 1720 by the botanist Pier Antonio Micheli. At around 306 years old, it is one of the few trees in the city whose exact planting date is on record rather than estimated.

faq.q: Are Florence's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Many are, and two paid gardens hold the rest. Free: the two Parco delle Cascine entries, the Bobolino and the incense cedar by its gate, Salviatino, Piazzale Michelangelo, Villa Vogel and the wisteria in the Esselunga forecourt on Via Pisana. Ticketed: the Giardino dei Semplici botanical garden and the Boboli Gardens, both ordinary museum-style tickets rather than anything charged for the trees. Seven of the newest entries have no access note yet and we would rather leave that blank than guess.

faq.q: Why are so few of Florence's remarkable trees medieval or older?
faq.a: Most of the city's oldest documented trees were planted deliberately inside institutional gardens, starting with the Giardino dei Semplici in 1545, rather than left standing through centuries of agriculture, flooding and war. Florence's real age is in its buildings; its trees are mostly eighteenth, nineteenth and early twentieth century plantings by comparison.

faq.q: What did Giuseppe Poggi have to do with Florence's trees?
faq.a: Poggi was the architect who redesigned Florence's hillsides and boulevards when the city briefly served as capital of unified Italy in the 1860s and 70s. Piazzale Michelangelo, the Bobolino garden and several of the trees on this list all date from that single decade of work.
